query: For high-value components operating in aggressive environments, what intervention could improve surface physical and mechanical characteristics? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence that would support it, and an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A layer‐gradient thermal barrier coating applied by detonation spraying, which uses alternating layers of NiCrAlY and yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), will significantly improve the surface physical and mechanical properties of high-value components in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Bare or conventionally coated metallic components (e.g., gas turbine parts) that are vulnerable to wear, corrosion, and thermal shock under high-temperature and corrosive conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a multilayer gradient coating using detonation spraying to deposit alternating layers of NiCrAlY and YSZ that gradually transition from a metallic bond coat to a ceramic thermal barrier.
generation.conditions: Operating at high temperatures (above 1000°C) with cyclic thermal loads in corrosive environments (e.g., exposure to 3.5% NaCl solution) and other aggressive media.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, low-porosity, layered structure with gradual compositional change and well-defined interphase boundaries; transformation of monoclinic ZrO2 to the more mechanically robust tetragonal phase that improves adhesion and decreases cracking.
generation.mechanism: The gradient coating minimizes thermal expansion mismatches between the metal and ceramic layers by providing a smooth transition in composition. This reduction in thermal stress accumulation improves the mechanical strength, wear resistance, and corrosion protection of the surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated components will exhibit higher hardness, lower wear rates, and improved corrosion resistance as well as better tolerance to thermal shocks compared with untreated or conventionally coated surfaces.
generation.baseline: Untreated surfaces or surfaces with single-layer homogeneous coatings that do not address the thermal expansion mismatch effectively.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only when the coating thickness is optimized; excessively thick gradient layers may experience peeling under prolonged thermal cycling.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal layer thicknesses and gradient profiles to balance adhesion and stress relief may vary depending on specific operational parameters, and further refinement is needed to adapt the coating for all aggressive conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate metallic test samples and apply the proposed gradient NiCrAlY/YSZ coating using detonation spraying with variable layer thicknesses. Subject the samples to cyclic high-temperature exposure (>1000°C) in a 3.5% NaCl solution to simulate aggressive conditions. Compare the performance of these samples against untreated or conventionally coated control samples.
measurements: Microhardness testing to evaluate surface hardness improvements
Tribological tests to measure wear rates
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to assess corrosion resistance
Microscopic examination for thermal shock-induced cracking or layer delamination
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the gradient coated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance compared to the controls, or if severe delamination/peeling of the coating is observed under standard thermal cycling conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThis paper presents the results of a study of layer gradient thermal protection coatings based on NiCrAlY and YSZ obtained by detonation spraying. Modern gas turbines and high-temperature units operate under extreme temperatures and aggressive environments, which requires effective protection of components from wear, corrosion, and thermal shocks. In this study, the use of layer gradient coatings consisting of alternating layers of NiCrAlY and YSZ was investigated with the aim of solving the problem of thermal stress accumulation due to a smooth change in the composition of the layers. Microstructural and phase analysis showed that alternating layers of NiCrAlY and YSZ formed a dense layer gradient structure with clear interphase boundaries and low porosity. Detonation spraying led to a complete transformation of the monoclinic ZrO2 phase into a tetragonal one, which significantly increased the mechanical strength of the coating and its resistance to thermal shocks. Sample 1D1 demonstrated excellent tribological and corrosion properties in a 3.5% NaCl solution, which can be explained by its higher density and reduced number of pores. The NiCrAlY (nickel–chromium–aluminum alloys) bonding layer forms a protective oxide layer, Al2O3, which effectively prevents further oxidation of the metal layer at high temperatures []. This improves thermal resistance and protects the metal from corrosion in aggressive environments, such as atmospheres with high chloride or sulfide content. Studies have confirmed that this material is highly resistant to oxidation and retains its mechanical properties at temperatures above 1000 °C []. Ceramic coating based on YSZ (stabilized zirconium oxide) plays the role of a thermal barrier due to its unique thermal insulation properties. Grains of tetragonal zirconia stabilized with yttrium oxide (Y2O3) prevent phase transformation and cracking under thermal cyclic stresses [].
